analysis.one_liner: Creates a traceback system to trace contaminated meat and poultry from consumer back to the farm.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past committee referral and died when the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal meat and poultry inspection laws to require that livestock and poultry be identified so the Agriculture Secretary can trace any animal back to every location it was held before slaughter, and trace any meat or poultry product forward from slaughter to the consumer. It would let the Secretary bar unidentified animals from slaughterhouses, require businesses to keep accurate records open to inspection, and make it a violation to falsify or destroy those records [S2] [S3]. The purpose is faster, more precise response when contamination outbreaks happen, instead of broad recalls and guesswork [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of meat and poultry. When a contamination outbreak occurs, regulators could pinpoint the exact farm, plant, and batch involved, allowing faster and narrower recalls and a better chance of finding the source of illness.

how_it_helps.text: Requires animals and meat products shipped in interstate commerce to be identified so the Secretary of Agriculture can trace each animal to any location where it was held before slaughter and each product forward through processing and distribution to the ultimate consumer [S2] [S3].
Lets the Secretary prohibit or restrict entry of unidentified animals into slaughterhouses, so uninspectable livestock cannot enter the food supply [S2] [S3].

Requires businesses handling covered livestock and poultry to keep accurate purchase, sale, and identification records, open to Agriculture Department inspection, with penalties for falsifying or destroying records [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The meatpacking and poultry processing industries, livestock producers, and others in the supply chain, who would bear the cost of animal identification, recordkeeping, and audits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Meatpackers, poultry processors, and livestock producers

drawbacks.text: The recordkeeping and identification requirements would impose new compliance costs on livestock producers, small farmers, and meat processors, and the bill leaves the details to Agriculture Department rules, so the burden's size is unknown [S3].
A full traceback system centralizes detailed business records with the federal government, which critics of animal-identification programs have historically opposed on cost and privacy grounds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real: traceability means faster, narrower recalls and better outbreak investigations, protecting people from foodborne illness. The costs fall on the meat industry and, at the margin, possibly consumers through prices, and the bill would have required considerable bureaucratic implementation. It was a moderate regulatory bill, not a sweeping overhaul, and the safety gains it targeted were genuine.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its Livestock and Horticulture Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Diana DeGette introduced the bill on June 29, 2006, with six Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S4].
The House referred it to the Agriculture Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
On July 10, 2006, it was referred to the subcommittee on Livestock and Horticulture, where it stayed; no further action was taken before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meatpacking and poultry processing companies and large livestock producers avoided new identification, recordkeeping, and audit requirements, while consumers gained no new traceback protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Meat and poultry processors who avoided new rules

for.name: Rep. Diana DeGette
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a meat and poultry traceability system and referred it to committee.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 29, 2006, and sent it to the Livestock and Horticulture Subcommittee, where it remained without a hearing or markup for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic sponsors and cosponsors, and it died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority without any recorded vote, so the partisan shape of opposition was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would require traceback-capable identification, records, and audits across slaughter, processing, and distribution, a compliance cost for an industry that in 2006 operated without it. Its interest in avoiding that cost ran against the public's interest in faster contamination recalls.

Producers would have to identify animals and maintain records of every premises where livestock was held. Some producers bear disproportionate paperwork costs, particularly smaller operations, though traceability can also protect markets during outbreaks.
